summary: Defines how an IKEv2 client and gateway can resume a previous session with fewer round trips and less cryptographic work. This helps remote-access VPNs where EAP authentication is expensive or a gateway fails over. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When a remote access client loses its connection to a VPN gateway, it normally has to start the whole handshake again, including checking the user's credentials. This RFC lets it resume instead. The gateway gives the client a small piece of protected data called a ticket, and the client sends that ticket back when it reconnects, so the gateway knows who it is talking to without asking for a password again.

questions: how does ikev2 session resumption work
how to reconnect a vpn without full authentication
ticket by value vs ticket by reference ikev2
subtitle: Letting a VPN client pick up a dropped session where it left off, without starting the whole handshake again.

tldr.problem: Re-establishing an IPsec session from scratch takes several round trips and a full authentication, which is slow for a remote access client and expensive for a gateway handling many clients.
tldr.mechanism: The gateway hands the client an opaque ticket carrying the previous session state, encrypted and integrity-protected in the ticket-by-value case or held on the gateway in the ticket-by-reference case. The client later presents the ticket in a new IKE_SESSION_RESUME exchange and confirms it with a normal IKE_AUTH exchange.
tldr.outcome: The resumed session gets fresh keys derived from the old session key and the new nonces, so the protection is as strong as a full handshake. Tickets are for one-time use and must be deleted when the session ends.

facts.label: Ticket lifetime
facts.value: the minimum of the IKE SA lifetime and the re-authentication time

today: RFC 5723 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. It is an extension to the IKEv2 protocol in RFC 4306, and it leaves the ticket format to the implementor while giving examples of both approaches in its Appendix A.

sections.title: Why Resume Instead of Starting Over
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange version 2 protocol has a computational and communication overhead in terms of the number of round trips required and the cryptographic operations involved. In remote access situations the Extensible Authentication Protocol is used for authentication, which adds several more round trips and consequently latency.

Re-establishing security associations upon a failure recovery condition is time-consuming, especially when an IPsec peer such as a VPN gateway has to re-establish a large number of SAs with various endpoints. A high number of concurrent sessions might cause additional problems for an IPsec peer during SA re-establishment, and usability is affected when the re-establishment of an IKE SA involves user interaction for re-authentication.

This document proposes an extension to IKEv2 that allows a client to re-establish an IKE SA with a gateway in a highly efficient manner, using a previously established IKE SA. The client, the IKEv2 initiator, stores the state about the previous IKE SA locally. The gateway, the IKEv2 responder, has two options for maintaining the state.

In the ticket by reference approach the gateway stores the state locally and gives the client a protected and opaque reference, for example an index into the gateway's table, which the gateway can later use to find the state. In the ticket by value approach the gateway stores its state in a ticket, a data structure that is encrypted and integrity-protected by a key known only to the gateway. The ticket is passed to the client, who treats it as an opaque string, and sent back to the gateway when the session is resumed, so the gateway can decrypt it and recover the state.

The client behaves identically in both cases and in general does not know which approach the gateway is using. Since the ticket or reference is interpreted only by the party that created it, the document does not specify an exact format for it, but Appendix A gives examples of both. The approach is similar to TLS session resumption, with the adaptations IKEv2 needs for its two-phase structure. The stated goals are to use only symmetric cryptography, to provide cryptographic agility, and to have no negative impact on IKEv2 security features. The non-goals are failover from one gateway to another, load balancing among gateways, and specifying how a client detects the need for resumption.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a protected connection from scratch takes several round trips and a lot of cryptography, and with a password prompt it can take even longer. This RFC lets a client that was disconnected pick up where it left off, using a small piece of data the gateway gave it earlier.

sections.title: Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
The specification envisions two usage scenarios. The first is like the use case in the IKEv2 specification, where IPsec tunnel mode is used to establish a secure channel between a remote access client and a gateway, and the traffic flow may be between the client and entities beyond the gateway. The second focuses on using transport or tunnel mode to secure the communication between two endpoints, such as two servers, where the two endpoints have a client-server relationship with respect to a protocol that runs using the protections afforded by the IPsec SA.

In the first use case an end host with a host implementation of IPsec establishes a tunnel mode IPsec SA with a gateway in a remote network using IKEv2. At a later stage, when the client needs to re-establish the IKEv2 session, it may choose to establish IPsec SAs using a full IKEv2 exchange or the IKE_SESSION_RESUME exchange.

The RFC lists several situations where the mechanism is useful. If a client temporarily loses network connectivity and the IKE SA times out through the liveness test facility, known as dead peer detection, the mechanism re-establishes the SA with less overhead in network, CPU and authentication infrastructure, and without requiring user interaction for authentication. If connectivity problems affect a large number of clients, as at a large remote access VPN gateway, then when connectivity is restored all the clients might reconnect almost simultaneously, and the mechanism reduces the load spike for cryptographic operations and authentication infrastructure. Losing connectivity can also be predictable and planned, for example putting a laptop into stand-by mode before travelling, and the mechanism re-establishes the SA when the laptop is switched back on. The RFC notes that such user-level resumption may often be disallowed by policy, and that this document requires the client to destroy the ticket when the user explicitly logs out.
sections.plainLanguage: The main case is a remote access client that lost its connection to a VPN gateway. The other case is two servers that keep a protected channel between them. Resumption helps most when many clients reconnect at once, because the gateway does far less work than if every client authenticated from scratch.

sections.title: Requesting and Receiving a Ticket
sections.content:
A client MAY request a ticket in several exchanges: in an IKE_AUTH exchange, which is the typical case; in a CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange when an IKE SA is rekeyed, and only when the client initiates that exchange; in an Informational exchange at any time, for example when the gateway previously replied with an acknowledgement instead of a ticket, when the ticket lifetime is about to expire, or following a gateway-initiated IKE rekey, all of which must be client-initiated; and while resuming an IKE session, in the IKE_AUTH exchange that follows an IKE_SESSION_RESUME exchange.

Normally the client requests a ticket in the third message of an IKEv2 exchange, the first of IKE_AUTH, by adding an N(TICKET_REQUEST) notification.

When a responder receives that request and supports the extension, it MUST do one of three things. It may create a ticket and return it with an N(TICKET_LT_OPAQUE) payload in a subsequent message. It may return an N(TICKET_NACK) if it refuses to grant a ticket for some reason. Or it may return an N(TICKET_ACK) if it cannot grant a ticket immediately, for example because of packet size limitations, in which case the client MAY request a ticket later using an Informational exchange at any time during the lifetime of the IKE SA. Whichever it does, there is no change to the behaviour of the responder with respect to the IKE exchange, and the proper IKE response, such as an IKE_AUTH response or an error notification, MUST still be sent.

The initiator receives the ticket and may accept it, provided the IKEv2 exchange was successful, and it may be used later with a responder that supports the extension. When a multi-round-trip IKE_AUTH exchange is used, the request MUST be included in the first IKE_AUTH request, and the ticket, nack or ack MUST only be returned in the final IKE_AUTH response. When the client accepts the ticket it stores it in its local storage for later use, along with the IKE SA to which the ticket refers. Since the ticket itself is opaque to the client, the local storage MUST also include all the items the RFC marks as coming from the ticket.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks for a ticket during the normal handshake, by adding a small notification to the third message. The gateway then either sends the ticket, refuses, or says it cannot do it now and will send it later. The client keeps the ticket with the details of the session it belongs to.

sections.title: Presenting the Ticket
sections.content:
It is up to the client's local policy to decide when communication with the responder is seen as interrupted and the resumption procedure is started. A client MAY initiate a regular, non-ticket-based IKEv2 exchange even if it is in possession of a valid, unexpired ticket, and it MUST NOT present a ticket when it knows that the ticket's lifetime has expired. Tickets are intended for one-time use: a client MUST NOT reuse a ticket, and a reused ticket SHOULD be rejected by a gateway. A ticket counts as used only when an IKE SA has been established successfully with it.

The RFC specifies a new IKEv2 exchange type called IKE_SESSION_RESUME, whose value is 38. It is equivalent to the IKE_SA_INIT exchange and MUST be followed by an IKE_AUTH exchange. The initiator sets the SPIi value in the header to a new, unique value and the SPIr value to 0. When the responder receives a ticket it MUST either accept it, responding with the SPIi copied from the request and a new, unique SPIr, or reject it for any reason with an unprotected N(TICKET_NACK), in which case the initiator should re-initiate a regular IKE exchange. One such case is a ticket for an IKE SA that the responder itself has previously terminated, which may indicate inconsistent state between the initiator and the responder.

Where not otherwise specified, the exchange behaves exactly like the IKE_SA_INIT exchange. The client MAY resume from any IP address and port, regardless of its original address, although the gateway MAY reject the exchange if its policy depends on the client's address. The first message MAY be rejected in denial-of-service situations, with the initiator instructed to send a cookie. Notifications normally associated with IKE_SA_INIT can be sent, in particular NAT detection payloads, and the client's NAT traversal status SHOULD be determined anew, because NAT status is explicitly not part of the session resumption state.

Following the IKE_SESSION_RESUME exchange the client MUST initiate an IKE_AUTH exchange. The AUTH payload is derived in a manner similar to IKEv2 pre-shared secret authentication, as AUTH = prf(SK_px, <message octets>), where each side uses its own value for SK_px, namely SK_pi for the initiator and SK_pr for the responder, both taken from the newly generated IKE SA. The IDi value sent in the IKE_AUTH exchange MUST be identical to the value included in the ticket, a CERT payload MUST NOT be included, and the IDr value sent by the gateway, and optionally by the client, MUST also be identical to the value included in the ticket. When the responder accepts the ticket and the IKE_AUTH exchange completes, the old SA SHOULD be silently deleted without sending a DELETE informational exchange, and consequently all the dependent IPsec Child SAs are also deleted.
sections.plainLanguage: To resume, the client sends the ticket in a short exchange that works like the first message of a normal handshake, then confirms the session in the usual authentication exchange. The ticket already carries the proof of identity, so no certificate or password is needed again.

sections.title: Generating Cryptographic Material for the Resumed IKE SA
sections.content:
The cryptographic material is refreshed based on the ticket and the nonce values Ni and Nr from the current exchange. A new SKEYSEED value is derived as SKEYSEED = prf(SK_d_old, "Resumption" | Ni | Nr), where SK_d_old is taken from the ticket and the literal string is encoded as 10 ASCII characters with no NULL terminator. The keys are then derived as they are in IKEv2, with {SK_d | SK_ai | SK_ar | SK_ei | SK_er | SK_pi | SK_pr} = prf+(SKEYSEED, Ni | Nr | SPIi | SPIr), where the SPI values are those created in the new exchange and the pseudorandom function is determined from the SA value in the ticket.

The RFC also tabulates the IKE and IPsec state after resumption and how it relates to the state before the IKE SA was interrupted. An item marked as coming from the ticket is retrieved by the client from its local store, encoded into the ticket by the gateway in the ticket-by-value case, or fetched by the gateway from the ticket store in the ticket-by-reference case. So IDi and IDr come from the ticket, as do the authentication method and, where applicable, the certificates. The NAT detection status and the SPIs come from the new exchange, the IKE SA sequence numbers are reset to 0 in IKE_SESSION_RESUME and then incremented normally, and the IKE SA algorithms come from the ticket. The IKE SA window size is reset to 1, Child SAs are created in the new exchange, and the internal IP address, other Configuration Payload information and the peer vendor IDs are not resumed.
sections.plainLanguage: The new keys are computed from the old session key and the random numbers in the new exchange, so both ends end up with fresh keys that nobody has seen before. The identity and the authentication method come from the ticket, but anything about the network connection is worked out again.

sections.title: Ticket Handling and Lifetime
sections.content:
When passing a ticket by value to the client, the ticket content MUST be integrity-protected and encrypted. A ticket by reference does not need to be encrypted, as it holds no sensitive material such as keying material, but access to the storage where that material is kept MUST be protected so that only authorised access is allowed. The RFC compares such a ticket to the stub concept and to a TLS session identifier. Although not strictly required for cryptographic protection, it is RECOMMENDED to integrity-protect a ticket by reference, because failing to do so could result in security vulnerabilities on the gateway side, depending on the format of the reference, such as the gateway accessing unintended URLs or SQL injection.

A ticket by value MUST encode all the state information marked as coming from the ticket, and the same state MUST be stored in the ticket store in the ticket-by-reference case. A ticket by value MUST include a protected expiration time, an absolute time value that SHOULD correspond to the value included in the TICKET_LT_OPAQUE payload, and it MUST additionally include a key identity field, so that the keys for ticket encryption and authentication can be changed and, when necessary, algorithms replaced.

Each ticket is associated with a single IKE SA. When an IKE SA is deleted by the client or the gateway, the client MUST delete its stored ticket, and when credentials associated with the IKE SA are invalidated, for example when a user logs out, the ticket MUST be deleted. When the IKE SA is rekeyed the ticket is invalidated and the client SHOULD request a new one.

The lifetime of the ticket sent by the gateway SHOULD be the minimum of the IKE SA lifetime, per the gateway's local policy, and its re-authentication time. Even if neither of these is enforced by the gateway, a finite lifetime MUST be specified for the ticket. The key used to protect the ticket MUST have a lifetime significantly longer than the lifetime of an IKE SA. In normal operation the client requests a ticket when establishing the initial IKE SA, and then every time the SA is rekeyed or re-established because of re-authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: A ticket is only good for one session and one try. The client has to throw it away when the session ends or when the user logs out, and the gateway has to give it an end date. The key that protects the ticket must live longer than any single session.

sections.title: The Notify Payloads
sections.content:
The RFC defines five notifications. The TICKET_LT_OPAQUE payload carries a ticket together with its remaining lifetime: it consists of the Notify message header, a Lifetime field and the ticket itself. The four octet Lifetime field contains a relative time value, the number of seconds until the ticket expires, encoded as an unsigned integer in network byte order. The TICKET_OPAQUE payload consists of the Notify message header and the ticket itself, with no lifetime value, and it is the payload the client sends back when it presents the ticket. TICKET_REQUEST, TICKET_ACK and TICKET_NACK carry no data.

For all of these notifications the Protocol ID and the SPI Size fields MUST both be sent as 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket travels in a small notification message. One kind carries the ticket and how long it stays valid, and another carries just the ticket, which is what the client sends back when it wants to resume.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A man in the middle may try to eavesdrop on an exchange to obtain a ticket by value and use it to establish a session with the responder. Since all the exchanges where the client obtains a ticket are encrypted, this is only possible by listening in on the client's use of the ticket to resume a session. Because the ticket's contents are encrypted and the attacker does not know the corresponding secret key, a stolen ticket cannot be used to resume a session successfully, and the responder MUST use strong encryption and integrity protection of the ticket. A ticket by reference cannot be used by an attacker to resume a session either, for the same reason, because the attacker would not be able to prove during IKE_AUTH its knowledge of the secret part of the IKE state embedded in the ticket. Access control must also ensure the reference is disclosed only to authorised entities.

A malicious user could forge or alter a ticket by value in order to resume a session, extend its lifetime, impersonate another user or gain additional privileges. This is not possible if the content is protected using a strong integrity protection algorithm. For a ticket by reference, an adversary may attempt to construct a fake reference pointing at state information stored by the responder, but the attack fails because the adversary is not in possession of the keying material associated with the IKE SA.

For denial of service, an adversary could send a large number of tickets by value to burden the gateway's CPU or exhaust its memory with half-open IKE state, so ticket verification should be lightweight and use efficient symmetric key algorithms. A large number of tickets by reference may lead to an amplification attack, because the responder is forced to resolve the reference to discover that the adversary holds no keying material, so the resolution protocol should be as lightweight as possible and should not generate a large number of messages. The regular IKEv2 cookie mechanism can be used for state-overflow denial-of-service situations.

On key management, the RFC recommends that the keys used to protect a ticket by value be generated securely following the randomness recommendations in RFC 4086, that the keys and cryptographic protection algorithms be at least 128 bits in strength, that the keys not be used for any other purpose than generating and verifying tickets, that the keys be changed regularly, and that they be changed if the ticket format or the algorithms change. A misbehaving client could present a ticket for an IKE SA that has already been deleted, so the gateway may maintain an Invalid Ticket List, a simple blacklist of revoked tickets, or use Bloom filters to keep the list in constant space; a policy requiring shorter ticket lifetimes, an hour for example, significantly mitigates the issue. Finally, since the IKE_SESSION_RESUME exchange provides no confidentiality, an on-path adversary could observe several exchanges that use the same state and conclude that they belong to the same endpoints, so this document requires the ticket to be presented to the responder only once.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket acts as proof that the client was here before, so it has to be protected like a password. If it is stolen it cannot be used, because the attacker cannot produce the matching keys, and it must not be used twice, because repeated use would let an observer link the sessions together.

messages.label: IKE_AUTH WITH TICKET REQUEST
messages.note: HDR, SK {IDi, AUTH, SAi2, TSi, TSr, N(TICKET_REQUEST)}

messages.label: IKE_AUTH WITH TICKET
messages.note: HDR, SK {IDr, AUTH, SAr2, TSi, TSr, N(TICKET_LT_OPAQUE)}

messages.label: IKE_SESSION_RESUME
messages.note: HDR, [N(COOKIE),] Ni, N(TICKET_OPAQUE). New SPIi, SPIr set to 0.

messages.label: IKE_SESSION_RESUME REPLY
messages.note: HDR, Nr [,N+]. The responder copies SPIi and sets a new SPIr.

messages.label: IKE_AUTH
messages.note: AUTH = prf(SK_px, message octets). The IDi and IDr values must match the ticket.

messages.label: IKE_AUTH REPLY
messages.note: The old SA is then silently deleted.

data.title: Deriving the new keys
data.code:
SKEYSEED = prf(SK_d_old, "Resumption" | Ni | Nr)

{SK_d | SK_ai | SK_ar | SK_ei | SK_er | SK_pi | SK_pr} =
    prf+(SKEYSEED, Ni | Nr | SPIi | SPIr)

items.desc: The client asks for a ticket. Carries no data.

items.desc: The gateway cannot issue a ticket right now. Carries no data.
